Commodities
•Oil. Brent settled around USD 103 a barrel on Wednesday, ending a five-session losing streak and reclaiming the USD 100 handle, while the front November contract trades at USD 102.30 this morning, down 0.8%. Concerns about a US diesel export ban eased after Energy Secretary Wright said voluntary export cuts were being sought instead, sending diesel futures sharply lower. WTI trades at USD 91.46, down 0.8%, leaving the Brent premium near USD 11. Meanwhile, conflicting signals continue to emerge from the Strait of Hormuz, where attacks on vessels persist despite Treasury Secretary Bessent saying that oil flows through the waterway have at times reached 17 million barrels per day.
•Metals. Precious metals fell on Wednesday, weighed down by a stronger dollar and renewed weakness in US Treasuries after robust PMI data and a weak five-year debt auction pushed yields to multi-year highs. Spot gold slipped below USD 4,300, while silver fell harder, dropping 4% on the day. Mining stocks bore the brunt of the broader equity-market weakness, with GDX down 4.36% and GDXJ 5.23%. Copper, meanwhile, held steady, supported by robust underlying demand fundamentals.
•Agriculture: Wheat futures fell to a one-month on hopes of easing Black Sea tensions, following diplomatic developments on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly as Russia flagged talks with mediator Turkey about ending strikes on grain vessels. Chicago wheat dropped as much as 1.5% and corn 1.4%. The market remains highly sensitive to the Black Sea conflict after an escalation since July disrupted the vital grain corridor, briefly driving wheat close to USD 8 per bushel and a three-year high, before prices retreated to around USD 7.06.

Recap of the EIA’s oil and fuel inventory report:

US crude inventories rose by 3 million barrels last week, largely reflecting a 1.6 mb/d drop in exports and a 0.5 mb/d decline in refinery inputs. SPR outflows slowed sharply to just 0.4 million barrels, while stocks at Cushing rose by 2 million barrels to their highest since May. Production held steady near an all-time high below 14 mb/d.

The headline crude build was somewhat distorted by an unexpected Midwest refinery shutdown caused by power outages. This reduced refinery demand for crude and contributed to a sharp drop in imports from Canada, a key source of supply to Midwest refiners.

Meanwhile, both distillate and gasoline inventories declined. Implied demand broadly followed seasonal patterns, rising for distillates while easing for gasoline. Closely watched distillate exports fell to around 1.3 mb/d from roughly 1.6 mb/d recently, potentially easing some of the political pressure surrounding US diesel exports at a time when domestic inventories remain tight.

We stay sharp in our 30’s and 40’s by visually identifying 52 tankers a day on satellite imagery while their AIS transponders are switched off.

The numbers have doubled in less than a month.

The total crude oil egress via the USN-BL is now 13 Mbpd, with estimated SoH transits at 10.35 Mbpd given that Fujairah and Mina al-Fahal together account for around 2.65 Mbpd on average.

This is partly attributed to Saudi Arabia having to swing back its exports eastwards due to pipeline disruption, but also due to daytime transits via the SoH under additional CENTCOM protection.

OK, so this is not how one tracks vessels in the Middle East. Most of the ones moving any cargo of value are keeping their AIS transponders switched off. Our month-on-month sightings show that Saudi Arabia's crude oil loadings along at its east coast are up sevenfold.
